en: The Mahāyāna Scripture on the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the State Preceptor Dharma-ratna,
the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Jñānaśrī, and others, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in due order; having received sufficient offerings, he returned to the Kalandaka Grove.
Having finished his meal, he sat cross-legged, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas who joyfully encircled him.

This great multitude had all attained dhāraṇīs that were equal and unimpeded; their minds realized total retention (saṃdhāraṇa), they attained samādhi, and they dwelt securely in the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They were endowed with immeasurable, sublime merits, such that neither speech nor thought could reach them.

Known and recognized by the multitude, they dwell in tranquility within such Dharma-gates; they are entirely equal toward all conceptual discriminations and do not follow the worldly preferences of the masses. Understanding the distinct natures of the consciousnesses of sentient beings, they remain at all times impartial toward what is known as good or evil, free from all hatred and attachment, and abiding in a single, uniform flavor of equality.

At that time, the World-Honored One suddenly emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows; the entire assembly was struck with awe and trembled, reverently joining their palms and gazing up at the Tathāgata without averting their eyes for even a moment.
The World-Honored One addressed them, saying:

"You should focus your minds in contemplation, abide in the sphere of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, and remain entirely free from notions of 'I' and 'mine,' as well as from likes, dislikes, and discrimination."

If one regards all experiences of suffering and pleasure—such as defamation and praise—with respect to oneself, and thoroughly understands that sentient beings, due to defiled conditions, undergo various distinct states and dwell in their preferred attachments day and night without ceasing, one shall, through the power of skillful means, cause them all to be completely severed.

He observes how sentient beings perform various kinds of unwholesome karma, following the instructions of others, vying with one another in their pursuits, and engaging in meaningless activities together with those of a similar class.
This arises because sentient beings possess minds that are ignorant and deluded, such that they lack understanding of the true realm;
they lose their superior wholesome mind and pursue evil companions.
Not understanding and not reflecting upon the profound and supreme Dharma;
giving rise to various conceptual discriminations regarding the truth of ultimate reality and taking them to be real;
and lacking discerning wisdom.
They lack firm confidence;
they do not give rise to a fondness for the Buddha’s teachings or for various sublime practices;
and even if they should practice virtue, it does not accord with correct principle.
Attachment to existence and attachment to emptiness are each taken as the ultimate by one another;
I am able to fully comprehend this through the power of the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom Samādhi.
You all should cultivate deep affection for them and feel great compassion.
When the great assembly heard this teaching, they praised the power of the Tathāgata’s supreme meditative concentration, which enables one to fully comprehend such distinctions.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then entered the *tathāgatajñānamudrā-samādhi*.

When this great assembly beheld the Buddha, the Tathāgata, entering this supreme meditative concentration, they suddenly could no longer see the physical marks and various characteristics of the Buddha’s body, nor could they comprehend them;
they likewise could not see or comprehend the Dharma robe and the inner garment worn by the Tathāgata;
and all the signs of the Tathāgata’s four modes of deportment, even down to every movement and gesture, became invisible and incomprehensible.
One cannot hear or comprehend the various distinctions of the Tathāgata’s speech. Why is this?
Because by dwelling in the supreme power of the merit of this Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, the mind is unmoving and unfathomable.

Furthermore, by means of his supreme power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Tathāgata causes all the various adornments of external objects and all the assembled multitudes to be invisible and unknowable;
likewise, he causes all the pure lands where he dwells to be unseen and unknowable.
Why is this? Because by virtue of the superior power of the merit of this samādhi, the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom, in which one dwells securely, the mind is unmoving and cannot be measured.
At that time, as the great assembly could no longer perceive the physical form of the Buddha, they each praised the merits of the supreme samādhi.
Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, their profound resolve sought liberation from all fears.
At that time, the Tathāgata again emitted a great radiance from within meditative concentration, which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm.
All the various lights therein—the light of the sun and moon, the stars, lightning, fire, medicinal herbs, and mani-jewels—were completely eclipsed.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, a distinct fragrance arose.
This fragrance was so subtle and exquisite that it could not be compared to worldly incenses such as sandalwood or aloeswood.

At that time, the gods of the form and formless realms, Brahmā, Śakra, and all other devas, humans, the fourfold assembly, and the eight classes of beings—along with those in the great Iron Ring Mountains, the small Iron Ring Mountains, Sumeru the king of mountains, and all the dark places of the water, land, and air realms—all beheld the radiance and marveled at this unprecedented wonder.
Each followed this light to the Kalandaka Grove and,
according to their respective means, offered incense, flowers, robes, jeweled crowns, and necklaces as acts of worship.

He saw the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas within this gathering, like lotuses in full bloom within a vast pond, their extraordinary fragrances wafting as they gathered together in the assembly.
At that time, when all the humans and devas smelled this fragrance, each of them attained clear and lucid wisdom.
Furthermore, precious necklaces and exquisite garments descended from the sky in every direction, providing solemn adornment and offerings.
At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with joy; they paid homage with reverence and withdrew to sit on one side.

Then, from the eastern direction, there were as many lands as there are grains of sand in ten koṭis of Gaṅgā rivers—each single grain of sand representing one koṭi—and all the Tathāgatas in those lands were emanations of Śākyamuni, appearing to transform and benefit sentient beings.
In this manner, each Tathāgata gathered an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering in the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and immeasurable.

These bodhisattvas had realized and attained equality; they were destined to obtain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and their physical forms and marks were so exquisitely perfected that none among the assemblies of devas and humans could equal them.
At that time, each of the Tathāgatas who had manifested as emanations addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!

In the Sahā world there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Śākyamuni, a Worthy One, a Perfectly Awakened One, who has appeared in the world to transform all sentient beings and cause them to leave behind the defilements of various sins."

Having expounded the True Dharma for immeasurable eons and revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—which are profoundly deep and difficult to understand—there is a dharani-gate called the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi-samāpatti; I shall now briefly praise and explain it for you.
"O sons of good family! Listen attentively!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have fully practiced the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; they possess great wisdom and immeasurable merit. They have realized and cultivated these practices without ever becoming weary or negligent, forever remaining free from the defilement of sin and abandoning all evil conditions. Abiding in samādhi, they have attained the wisdom of the Buddha; their minds are unshakable, and with this unshakable mind, they have awakened to all dharmas."

If all sentient beings were to draw near to the Tathāgata and the great Bodhisattvas, cultivate wisdom, show reverence through the three karmas, and perform various offerings with the wealth of the sublime Dharma for immeasurable time, it would not equal the merit obtained by abiding in such a supreme samādhi for even a single kṣaṇa; the latter cannot be compared to the former, and one will always be born in the superior lands of the Buddha-fields.

At that time, after the Buddhas had spoken these words, they entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and, by means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), gathered the bodhisattvas and proceeded to the Sahā world. Manifesting as a single body, they entered the city of Rājagṛha and went on almsround in succession. Having received sufficient offerings, they proceeded to the Kalandaka Grove, where they shared the exquisite offerings with the assembled multitude.
The entire assembly was fully satisfied.
Having finished eating, they gathered up their robes and bowls and sat down cross-legged.
All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who had come from all lands did likewise; there was no difference between them, nor any distinction.

Furthermore, in the southern direction, there are as many lands as there are grains of sand in one *koṭi* of *gaṅgā* rivers—where each single grain of sand constitutes one *koṭi*. All the Buddhas in those lands gather together with all the bodhisattvas they have gathered from those countries; the number is likewise the same.

Just as it was in the east and the south, so it was in the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; all the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas likewise gathered together in assembly.

At that time, Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, seeing that all the emanated Buddhas had gathered together, felt great joy in his heart; for it is only between Buddha and Buddha that they are able to behold one another.

At that time, all the Tathāgatas entered together into the samādhi and samāpatti of the Seal of Wisdom (jñānamudrā). Their minds became tranquil and vast, and all agitation ceased. With unmoving minds, they clearly illumined all phenomena as non-dual and undifferentiated; even the physical marks of the Buddhas no longer appeared.

At that time, the great assembly of humans and devas in this gathering saw the innumerable Buddhas of the ten directions all come to assemble; yet, through the power of their supreme meditative concentration, their physical forms did not appear. All were filled with wonder and joy; they adjusted their robes, joined their palms, and circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, offering in worship precious lotuses and various exquisite flowers endowed with every color.

At that time, the great bodhisattvas gathered from immeasurable worlds—those who had attained the pure mind, possessed the eye of the true Dharma, whose mental states were at all times serene and tranquil, and each of whom was destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni together with the other Tathāgatas, abiding in the samādhi and samāpatti of the Seal of Wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*). Through the power of their supreme concentration, they caused all physical forms to vanish; with aspirations and yearnings, their hearts filled with profound joy, and through the power of their refined attention, they did not rise from their seats. With awakened wisdom manifest before them, they entered the realm of the Buddhas and attained the gates of dhāraṇī.
Then those bodhisattvas addressed the great assembly in this Sahā world, saying:
"Sons of good family!
You should yearn for and longingly seek the virtues of the Buddha."
They direct their minds toward all sentient beings with compassion;
they know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have practiced the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, possess great wisdom, and have immeasurable merit and virtue;
and they fully understand all dharmas.
Free from all conceptual proliferation, dwelling in profound meditative concentration;
neither forgetful nor deluded, one thoroughly penetrates all natures and characteristics;
regarding this supreme Dharma, one should aspire to seek it.

At that time, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the trichiliocosm, who possessed great wisdom and had attained great supernormal powers, had abandoned the shore of birth and death, were freed from the bonds of affliction, and had fully realized and perfected their own nirvāṇa.

The great assembly of bhikṣus, along with various ministers, brahmins, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all such multitudes as these—came together here to the Karanda Grove in the great city of Rājagṛha, where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni and his assembly of emanation Buddhas were gathered. They circumambulated them hundreds of thousands of times, paying respectful homage and prostrating themselves. Each offered superior and exquisite lotuses of various colors, each with a thousand petals interspersed with the seven precious gems, surpassing in number the immeasurable to serve as an offering.

Furthermore, there was a multitude of eighty koṭi-nayuta great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; all these Bodhisattvas had been dispatched as messengers by the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, from lands in other directions. Possessing great valor, they were not terrified of birth and death; possessing great compassion, they did not delight in nirvāṇa. Each, by means of their supernatural powers, entered into great meditative concentration and manifested various majestic demeanors.

From each of those lands, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, they arrived at the Kalandaka Grove in Rājagṛha before the Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the assembly of his emanation Buddhas; there, with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, they paid homage and offered respectful praise with pure and wondrous voices.

Seeing that the bodies of the Buddhas were obscured and not manifest, they yearned for the World-Honored One; surrounding the assembly, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, withdrew to one side, and each sat cross-legged upon a precious lotus flower.

Furthermore, there were three hundred million bhikṣus who delighted in cultivating their own benefit and sought liberation; empowered by the Tathāgata’s samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, they gathered together.

At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, Maheśvara, the sons of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the sun, moon, and stars, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, humans, and non-humans, each together with their retinues, beheld the Buddha’s radiance and all assembled there.

This multitude is like this: suppose there were a person whose hair was thick and long; if one were to cut each single strand of hair into pieces as small as motes of dust—just as with the hair of one person, so too with the hair of ten million people—and were to take each mote of dust from a single strand of hair to represent a single sentient being, the assembly gathered here would still exceed that number.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahāpūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahāsūbhūti, and others, perceived that although the great assembly was present in the gathering, they could not behold the physical form and color of the Tathāgata, nor his dwelling place.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, approached the presence of the youthful Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and said: "O Noble One!
Now that the World-Honored One has entered this Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi, why is it that we are unable to see the body of the Tathāgata and his dwelling place?"
Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"You śrāvakas possess great wisdom, have attained all liberations, constantly practice the holy life, are free from all fears, and are revered by all humans and devas."
"You all should each, relying upon the samādhi-gates you have individually attained, use the power of wisdom to observe the physical form and dwelling place of the Tathāgata.

At that time, Śāriputra and the others immediately each entered their respective samādhi-gates and, using the power of wisdom, observed and sought the Tathāgata’s physical body and his dwelling place throughout every atom-dust land within the trichiliocosm; yet, even exhausting all their supernatural powers, they were unable to see him.
Then Śāriputra addressed the Youthful Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"Relying upon the gateways of samādhi that we have each attained, we have used the power of our wisdom to observe and seek the form-body (rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata and his dwelling place, yet we could not perceive them at all."
"I only pray that the Benevolent One will analyze and point this out for our sake, so that we may all behold it!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"Although you śrāvakas possess wisdom and supernatural powers, you are unable to contemplate the Tathāgata’s Samādhi-gate of the Seal of Wisdom; therefore, you are unable to see the Buddha’s body or his dwelling place."
Why is this so? You śrāvakas, with your discriminating minds, perceive the dwelling place of the Tathāgata’s form-body; through this conceptualization, you create obstacles for yourselves.

This body of the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by a discriminating mind. If your own body were the very body of the Tathāgata, and your dwelling place were the very dwelling place of the Tathāgata—extending even to the point that the bodies of all sentient beings are the very body of the Tathāgata and the dwelling places of all sentient beings are the very dwelling place of the Tathāgata; if you perceive the identity of emptiness and existence, and the non-duality of self and other; if you realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) without abandoning the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and awaken to the conditioned without departing from the unconditioned—then, by observing the body and dwelling place of the Tathāgata with such a mind, you shall finally be able to see them.

Since you all employ a mind of conceptual discrimination while desiring to see the signless realm of the Tathāgata, even if you were to pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, you would still be unable to attain it.

Thereupon, the assembly was moved by grief and distress; they relinquished their discriminative thoughts and dwelt securely in right mindfulness, remaining as tranquil as space both internally and externally, in body and mind.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration; his mind was as vast as the surging ocean, clear and translucent like pure lapis lazuli, universally observing sentient beings—whether their bodies or their lands—as equal and non-dual with all Tathāgatas.
The physical form was vast and clear, visible to the entire assembly.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook violently.
All the devas rejoiced greatly, free from all fear, and rained down celestial jewel-flowers from the midst of the void; those flowers were exquisite and fell in profusion.

Furthermore, celestial music was performed in the air, with various songs and sublime sounds from lutes, harps, *konghou*, *pipa*, flutes, and pipes; these musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, serving as an offering within this assembly.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, approached the World-Honored One, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!
Regarding the Tathāgata’s entry into the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, we were entirely unaware of it.

Each of us, by means of our own supernormal powers, entered the gateways of samādhi attained through our respective efforts; yet, though we searched everywhere with the power of our wisdom for the Tathāgata’s physical form and his dwelling place, they remained utterly unfindable, and we could not comprehend them.

It is because our own previously attained gateways of samādhi and power of wisdom were narrow, inferior, and limited; we had not yet attained the Tathāgata’s gateway of the sovereign dharma of signless, correct wisdom.

We only pray that the World-Honored One, through the power of great compassion, will deeply extend your pity and provide guidance for us, leading us to awaken to and enter the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as well as his concentration and wisdom, so that the realm of formlessness may spontaneously manifest before us.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:

"I have entered this samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (jñānamudrā-samādhi), which cannot be understood or investigated by the wisdom attained by you śrāvakas or any pratyekabuddhas; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it."

Why is this? The physical body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata arises from a mind free from movement; it is detached from all seeking, has abandoned the conditions of conceptual discrimination, and has severed the marks of self and other. It is immovable and profoundly tranquil, sustained by the power of supreme wisdom, and its essential characteristic is its identity with the suchness (*tathatā*) of great meditative concentration.

If you Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas seek only your own benefit and do not delight in benefiting others; if the Dharma-gates and the objects of wisdom you have realized have not yet attained mutual integration; if there is a separation between self and others and a mutual contradiction between emptiness and existence, then it will be difficult for you to understand and enter the Buddha-Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom regarding the Emptiness and Signlessness of Dharmas.
Therefore, you are unable to see the physical marks and characteristics of the Buddha’s body, nor his dwelling place, and you do not understand them.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“The merits attained by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, whether through body or mind, are difficult to cultivate, difficult to realize, and difficult to penetrate. Why is this?
Śāriputra! When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, observe various forms with their eyes, this consciousness is not moved by the objective realm of form;
when they hear various sounds with their ears, this consciousness is not moved by the objective realm of sound.
When the nose smells various fragrances, this consciousness is not moved by the object of fragrance;
when the tongue tastes various flavors, this consciousness is not moved by the object of flavor;
when the body perceives various tangibles, this consciousness is not moved by the object of tangibility.

Why is this? Because they possess mastery over consciousness and wisdom, they do not falsely discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly regarding external objects, nor do they give rise to attachment or aversion. "Śāriputra!..."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take all phenomena as objects of their mental focus; through association with supreme wisdom, they thoroughly understand that which is observed: that arising is non-arising, and thus they attain the most supreme non-arising;
that tranquility is non-tranquility, and thus they attain the most supreme tranquility;
that meditative concentration is non-concentration, and thus they attain the most supreme meditative concentration.
Discipline and non-discipline—this is the attainment of the supreme discipline;
conceptual proliferation and non-proliferation—this is the transcendence of the supreme proliferation;
discrimination and non-discrimination—this is the transcendence of the supreme discrimination.
"Annihilation and non-annihilation—this is the attainment of the supreme annihilation. Śāriputra!
Whatever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have spoken is free from all falsehood; there is nothing therein that is not true."
Its meaning and flavor are abundant, bringing an end to disputes;
its mental characteristics are equal, free from all disparate and unequal phenomena;
it enables those who hear it to eliminate evil desires, not give rise to wrong views, and abandon perverse thoughts.

Śāriputra! Regarding that which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas have realized, there is neither going nor coming; it is neither eternal nor discontinuous; it is neither empty nor existent; it is free from seeing and free from hearing; it has no form of large or small, and no characteristics of square or round.
“Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the perfection of the characteristics and nature of the path that can be realized, and the radiance of wisdom;
they are far removed from both distinct characteristics and non-distinct characteristics.”
It is devoid of both discernment and non-discernment;
its essence is like a vajra, for it is indestructible;
its function is like space, for it is free from grasping and rejecting.
They have no attachment to superior wholesome dharmas;
they have no fear regarding vast practices;
their mental states are empty and tranquil, free from discourse, hearing, and seeing.

“Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide in the supreme meditative concentration of the ultimate limit, which is pure and perfect; they do not weary of the bustle of the world, nor do they delight in empty stillness;
at all times, they constantly sport therein.”
He fully realizes the distinctions between the Dharma and non-Dharma, as well as between sentient beings and their physical environments;
his meditative concentration is so firm that it remains exactly as it is according to the object,
remaining indestructible even when encountering adverse conditions.

“Śāriputra! For all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the noble and wealthy realms of all worldly pleasures are like dreams, like illusions, and like discarded footprints; they do not seek anything by relying on ministers, officials, or great Brahmins. Therefore, they are not bound by fame or gain.”

“Śāriputra! Whether the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas hear sounds from sentient beings or non-sentient things, they do not give rise to distinctions based upon them, and they are likewise far removed from a mind of non-distinction.”

“Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not give rise to resolute conviction regarding the determinate objective aspects of any objects of perception; they are likewise far removed from a mind of resolute conviction.”

“Śāriputra! At all times, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not calculate duration or brevity, exhaustion or non-exhaustion, formation or destruction, or difference; they are likewise far removed from a mind of non-difference.
They thoroughly understand that all phenomena are ineffable, unspeakable, and devoid of past, future, or present.”
Within the mind and mental factors, there is neither association nor dissociation;
all conceptualization and recollection fail to arise;
there is no this shore, and there is no other shore.
"Regarding all sentient beings and their environments, there are none who are superior, middling, or inferior;
their profound resolve is firm and solid, and cannot be destroyed. Śāriputra!"
The physical forms of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are devoid of movement and free from all worldly activities;
toward those who are hateful or hostile, and those who are faithful or affectionate, they maintain an impartial compassion that renders the manifest and the hidden non-dual.

Because in former causal stages he had abandoned boundless hindrances and cultivated boundless practices, bestowing the wisdom of great compassion upon all sentient beings; through authentic observation, he was fully capable of benefiting them according to what was appropriate for each, causing all sentient beings to find joy and fulfillment in accordance with their respective aspirations.
Therefore, regarding the physical marks and wisdom thus attained, they are known only through self-realization, with nothing else to be understood;

his own bodily form is without limit, equal to space, neither hidden nor manifest, pervading all things, adorned by the power of supreme merits, complete with the primary and secondary marks, without any deficiency;
he exists neither within nor outside the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
Regarding all the activities practiced by sentient beings, they are able to relinquish them entirely, except for those manifested through the wisdom of skillful means;
their inner mind is pure, and their external appearance is pure.
“Śāriputra! As has been described above, all these are the marks of the Tathāgata’s adornment with the supreme, virtuous merits of both body and mind, which are pervasive and equal.”
If you seek to see the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body—which is sustained by his supreme meditative concentration—with your own discriminating minds, that body of the Tathāgata cannot be seen.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Tathāgata’s perfection of the form-body (rūpakāya) is termed ‘signless’ (animitta)?”
"What is the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom that is all-pervasive and equal?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The marks of the Tathāgata’s body and mind Are produced by meditative concentration and wisdom."
Not dependent on the牵引 (attraction) of external objects, the consciousness-characteristics do not stir through discrimination.
When the mind conditions all phenomena, it is no different from the body;
free from the distinctions of right and wrong, that which is attained is the most supreme.
If, with a mind of limited wisdom, one wishes to see the body of the Sugata—
like the moon’s reflection in the clear sky— and falsely claims it appears in water;
though the physical marks are inherently subtle and further sustained by supreme meditative concentration, [they cannot be seen thus].
Free from long, short, square, or round, Without coming, going, staying, or standing;
The inner mind is tranquil and unmoving, Serene and still as empty space.
With the cessation and dissolution of the marks of body and mind, It is naturally nothing at all.
With a mind of non-existence, One does not cling to fragrance, flavor, or touch;
Detached from the aggregates, bases, and elements, In this way one contemplates the Tathāgata.
Like seeing the moon in water, Though it cannot be grasped as real,
Once one is free from the conceptualizing mind, this too is called "seeing.
This gateway of the Tathāgata’s seal of wisdom is not something I alone can realize;
if there are beings of great resolve who seek it with tireless aspiration, [they may attain it].
One attains the most supreme dhāraṇī; by relying on this power of superior concentration, one shall likewise attain non-apprehension regarding the gateway of the Buddha’s Wisdom Seal.
The merit produced by this sutra is inexhaustible, like space.
By means of my wisdom of skillful methods, I have praised it briefly and in summary.

If one were to take all the various precious jewels that fill the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions and offer them as a gift, [it would not equal the merit of this praise].
If one were to spend immeasurable eons copying or upholding [this sutra],
the merit obtained by such a person would exceed that of the former donor of gifts by a factor greater than the number of sands in the Ganges.
If a person practices a mind of loving-kindness To benefit all sentient beings,
It is not equal to relying on this sutra To awaken to the Buddha’s samādhi. If,
within the realm of sentient beings, One’s mind constantly practices patience,
It is not equal to practicing a sublime concentration for even the duration of a finger-snap.
The merit thereby produced is like Mount Sumeru;
compared to a mote of dust, their great and small sizes cannot be matched.
If a person practices diligence and performs various good deeds with valor,
it is not equal to hearing this sutra and awakening to its principles according to the teachings;
the merit thus obtained [far exceeds] a hundred thousand million billion parts.
If one were to compare them by calculation, they would not equal even a fraction of it.
If a person cultivates meditative concentration, dwelling securely for immeasurable eons—
whether sitting, lying down, or walking— they pervade all Buddha-fields.
It is not equal to the merit of hearing this sutra for even a single moment.
Even if one were able to cultivate wisdom throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
severing the entanglements of afflictions and gaining renown that spreads everywhere, [it would still not equal the merit of hearing this sutra].
It is not equal to spending even a single kṣaṇa praising the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom-seal,
which is like comparing a single drop of water to the waters of the great ocean.
Those who wish to contemplate the Buddha must depart from all names and signs.
To thoroughly understand the nature of all phenomena, It is neither empty nor existent.
If one understands only emptiness, Even if one were like Subhūti,
One would still have no realization or entry Into the gateway of the Buddha’s Seal of Wisdom.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"Regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi as I have explained it, if bodhisattvas wish to fulfill unimpeded wisdom within the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, they should practice and study this stage of samādhi. Day and night they should apply themselves with diligence, dwelling peacefully in body and mind without distraction, never becoming weary or negligent."
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see all the Tathāgatas in all the Buddha-lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they will be able to see them all.

Śāriputra! This samādhi is the immeasurable and boundless, most supreme dharma-gate and profound dharma-eye of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it attains non-obstruction regarding all dharmas, penetratingly understands them, and is without any forgetfulness. This is called the Tathāgata’s most supreme dhāraṇī-door of total retention.

"If bodhisattvas desire to perfect all characteristics of discourse and wish to achieve the subtle and wondrous essence of unsurpassed enlightenment, they should with sincere resolve diligently practice and study this Dharma-gate of the Samādhi-Jñāna-Mudrā."

"If all bodhisattvas, according to their desire, distance themselves from all unwholesome karmic actions, they will be free from obstacles and achieve the most supreme and pure dharmas. By the power of wisdom, they will subdue hostile Māras, remain far removed from the unwholesome, and attain equality in all marks. Like the Tathāgata’s wisdom, they will be free from all defilement; with all karmic obstructions exhausted, they will be pure and stainless."
Abiding in the Tathāgata’s stage of ultimate wisdom, they are able to cause all evils and all demonic adversaries to be completely stilled, remaining unshakable;

with clear and lucid awakened intelligence, they know the various conceptualizations, the objects of attachment and delight, and the distinctions between the causes, conditions, and fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma of all sentient beings;
they thoroughly understand the subtle mental states and the fetters of affliction of all sentient beings, and being skillfully able to know them, they liberate all sentient beings from every bond.
One should study and practice this Dharma-gate of the Seal of Wisdom of the Supreme Samādhi of Skillful Means as taught by the Tathāgata.

"If bodhisattvas wish to cause sentient beings to become firm in their aspirations and resolve, and to desire contemplation and seek the unsurpassed Dharma, they should diligently cultivate such a gate of samādhi; thus, the supreme and unsurpassed Dharma will be spontaneously accomplished."

“If bodhisattvas wish to proclaim for all sentient beings the various teachings that serve as remedies for the diseases of their diverse faculties and dispositions, they should diligently cultivate such gateways of samādhi; then, they will naturally expound and explain these dharmas with discernment and without obstruction.”

"If bodhisattvas desire, with their minds, to discern and clearly awaken to the profound meaning of the phenomena of the true and conventional truths within the noble Dharma of the three vehicles, they should diligently practice such samādhi gates; thus, they will naturally attain clear wisdom regarding the Dharma and will not give rise to dullness."

"If bodhisattvas wish to fully comprehend, throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, that [all things] are subject to arising and ceasing, are illusory transformations, and lack solidity, and if they wish to realize the true intrinsic nature of all phenomena and attain pure liberation, they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi."

"If Bodhisattvas wish to personally awaken to the causes of arising and ceasing within the twelve links of dependent origination—beginning with ignorance, which gives rise to karmic formations and gathers in the retribution of suffering; wherein craving, attachment, and sensual desire increase and flourish; and through the provisional aggregation of existence, the characteristics of birth, death, and illness are formed—a state that is subject to change and impermanence as it transmigrates through the various realms—they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi."

"If bodhisattvas wish to thoroughly understand all various classes of sentient beings—their arising of views, their performance of karma, the distinctions in the characteristics of their retributions, the clarity or dullness of their consciousness, their correct mindfulness or inverted thoughts, and their diverse natures—and wish to know, as they truly are, the sharpness or dullness of their faculties so as to provide skillful instruction and gradually lead them to awaken to and enter the true, sublime Dharma, abiding in the stage of practice through faith, they should diligently cultivate this supreme samādhi."

"If Bodhisattvas wish to achieve the pure karmic causes for all Buddha-fields and realms of pure goodness, and desire their own bodies and minds to be tranquil, their retinues to be harmonious, and to remain far removed from the faults of envy and arrogance; and if they wish to cultivate intimacy and respect, to love others with equanimity, and to be free from thoughts of enmity or hatred, they should diligently practice such a supreme samādhi."

"If Bodhisattvas desire to give rise to the sublime and wondrous radiance of their own wisdom, to illuminate the darkness and the heavy veils of ignorance within the birth-and-death of themselves and others, to sever the delusions of the three realms, to extinguish all retributive suffering, and to attain sovereign liberation, they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi."

"If Bodhisattvas wish to know all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions—where they die here and are reborn there, the duration of their lifespans, the long kalpas and the moments of birth and death that pass, and how these are all induced by the power of the attraction of prior karma—and if they wish to understand as it truly is the homogeneous karmic results and the fundamental basis of their determined lifespans, they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi."

"If Bodhisattvas wish to know the sublime practices performed by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas from their respective stages of the path—including the abandonment and realization regarding the Four Noble Truths, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, the subtle and profound self-awakening in stillness, and the pure causal practices of the ten *pāramitās* through which each attains ultimate fruition—they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi."

“If bodhisattvas wish to respond appropriately and in a timely manner to all speech, sounds, debates, and eloquent arguments—responding without negligence or error, with skillful means, clearly manifesting both the conventional and the ultimate so that others may easily understand, without giving rise to doubt, and reaching a definitive certainty—they should diligently cultivate such a supreme samādhi.”

"If bodhisattvas wish to thoroughly understand the true cause of the Buddha-dharma, to accord with the skillful means of the wholesome practices of the three vehicles, and to enter the stage of the bodhisattva grounds in accordance with the nature of reality—distinguishing between the superior, middling, and inferior roots, gradually cultivating through perfuming, planting all roots of goodness, and attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata—they should diligently practice such a supreme samādhi."

“If bodhisattvas desire to achieve the perfect awakened wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, they should give rise to no conceptual discrimination, manifesting various bodies and spontaneously embracing all sentient beings with impartial compassion so that each may give birth to joy and take delight in practicing and learning the conduct and vows of the Bodhisattva Ground; they should thus diligently cultivate this supreme samādhi.”
“Śāriputra! The dharma of samādhi as I have taught it is the most supreme;
like a maṇi jewel, whatever all sentient beings desire, they shall obtain according to their wishes, with none left unsatisfied.”

Śāriputra! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain this dharma of the Tathāgata’s samādhi, they will obtain all necessary dharmas, noble wealth, and subtle practices exactly as they wish, and their conduct and vows will be fulfilled.
"Therefore, you should practice with diligent effort.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata Is supreme and beyond compare; No other is its equal."
According to the distinctions of the characteristics of phenomena, one is able to realize them all.
Through the light of the wisdom of equality, which universally illuminates all fetters and attachments,
one can enter the gateway of wisdom and attain immeasurable mastery.
The characteristics of wisdom and the nature of wisdom can certify all phenomena;
they distinguish between good and evil, as well as the conventional and the ultimate.
One who clearly understands such dharmas possesses wisdom that is inexhaustible.
Just as the great sun, when it rises, Shines its light throughout the three realms, Universally destroying all darkness,
And accomplishing the Dharma of equality.
All samādhis arise from the seal of wisdom;
they are called the seed of all Buddhas, and are also named the Great Maṇi,
benefiting all sentient beings.
There is a most supreme treasure, Whose wealth is inexhaustible;
It relieves all who are poor and destitute, Causing them all to attain sufficiency.
Bestowing the wealth of the Dharma upon sentient beings, It likewise remains inexhaustible.
Supernormal powers and wisdom, The most supreme and wondrous Dharma-gate,
All arise from samādhi, Born from the jewel of the seal of knowledge.
Just as in various lands, There is a great maṇi-jewel;
All kings cherish it, and ministers and officials everywhere protect and uphold it;
such a maṇi jewel is unsurpassed among all jewels.
I speak of the Jewel of the Seal of Wisdom, which is most excellent and supreme.
The light of the wisdom of dhāraṇī destroys all views;
its objects are fully understood, and it remains far removed from all darkness.
Abiding in a tranquil mind, one does not discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly.
Cultivating pure wisdom, with inexhaustible wealth and Dharma,
free from the stains of craving and attachment, devoid of the sixty-two views,
with right mindfulness in total equanimity, they enter the gateway to the Deathless.
One swiftly attains the wisdom of the Tathāgata, Accomplishing a body endowed with the marks and signs,
complete with the thirty-two characteristics, And attaining the most supreme enlightenment.
Equal to the awakening of all Buddhas, Sublime wisdom is already perfected and luminous.
Having reached the other shore of enlightenment, Realizing the intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa,
Possessing the perfection of self and others, All virtues are fully accomplished.
The immeasurable and boundless, Profound and subtle Dharma—
Through the dhāraṇīs of total retention, they are liberated in eternal tranquility.
They are able to fulfill the ten powers, and furthermore, by means of an ocean of great vows,
they practice the perfection of giving, as well as ethical discipline and patience.
Diligence and meditative concentration, with wisdom ever firm;
dwelling securely within the six perfections, for a long time without interruption;
free from all fears, one is liberated from afflictions, suffering, and karma.
Māra and his retinue cannot find an opportunity against them.
They are able to guide sentient beings, never abandoning the True Dharma;
they gradually enter the family of the Tathāgata and attain the gateway of the Seal of Wisdom.
Throughout this Bhadrakalpa and across the worlds of the ten directions, they draw near to all the assemblies of Buddhas and rejoice in them all.
Such a person is called a true child of the Buddha; no one can destroy them.
If there are those with faith and understanding who can transcribe this sutra,
or read, recite, and uphold it; who delight in its widespread dissemination for a long time without weariness, and who clearly comprehend its meaning and flavor;
One should know that such a sūtra as this is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
it gives birth to the jewels of the wisdom-seal and is the treasury of the Tathāgata’s merits.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Wisdom-Seal, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma Master Bao Fa,
the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Jñānaśrī, and others, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, there were also in the assembly as many Bodhisattvas as the sands of the Ganges, numbering in the nayutas; upon hearing the Buddha-Tathāgata preach this samādhi, they were freed from all obstacles and their minds attained liberation.
They entered into the profound and secret dhāraṇī teachings according to their inclination, realizing them with clarity and definitively upholding them.

Furthermore, there were sixty-eight nayutas of bodhisattvas who, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, had already cultivated meditative concentration and liberation; they were free from all false conceptualizations, the cycle of birth and death, and fear, and constantly delighted in practicing subtle and supreme conduct. Upon hearing this most sublime dharma of samādhi, their hearts leaped with joy; they attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, realized the sound of dhāraṇī and eloquence, and obtained unimpeded understanding.

Furthermore, there were sixty billion devas and humans who, upon hearing the Buddha’s exposition of the Dharma-gate of the Wisdom Seal, rejoiced immeasurably. They paid homage, praised him with reverence, prostrated, and made offerings; they conceived a deep affection for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, became free from doubt regarding the profound and supreme dharmas of *samādhi*, and all gave rise to faith and understanding.
They remained firm and steadfast in their bodhicitta, never abandoning it, and applied themselves with courageous diligence toward the gateway of the Wisdom Seal.

By the power of their great vows, they cultivate the roots of all virtues; as their faculties and nature reach maturity, they abide in the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression). They faithfully accept the practices and vows performed by the Tathāgata, their minds becoming resolute and free from all discouragement or regression.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the roots of goodness and their causal conditions had fully ripened, and wishing to bestow upon them a prediction of enlightenment, addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

After you have passed thirty billion kalpas from now, each of you shall fully cultivate the six pāramitās in various buddha-fields; all difficult practices, supreme vows, and deeds shall be completely fulfilled and accomplished.
When their seeds and habitual tendencies are both exhausted, they shall attain great bodhi and all become Buddhas, sharing the same title: Tathāgata Abhaya.

You, O assembly of devas and humans, and you sons of good family, have already planted many roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past and have placed your faith and joy in the Mahāyāna.
Now, having heard such a subtle, profound, and rare Dharma within this assembly, you shall joyfully accept and uphold it.
O sons of good family!
From this point forward, after the passing of billions of kalpas, you shall all together attain Buddhahood, each becoming identical to the Tathāgata Jñānamudrā.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had bestowed the prophecy of Buddhahood upon this bodhisattva and the assembly of devas and humans, he surveyed the entire gathering and addressed the youthful Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva with a gentle voice:

"I observe that although the bodhisattvas and devas in this assembly have each conceived a firm resolve for supreme enlightenment and are courageous and non-regressive, they are yet unable to establish the True Dharma within the path of false views during that final age."
Only you are able, during this time of the five turbidities within the trichiliocosm, to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;

through skillful means, you protect them, analyze and expound the teachings, and cause them to be widely disseminated everywhere, so that they may be freed from falsehood and all defilements of craving, and remain unbound by the pursuit of fame.

At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, composed his countenance, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and offered various flowers as an act of worship. Gazing up at him and praising him with a sense of unprecedented wonder, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent! "
"Bhagavān! As I observe all dharmas, none of them can be apprehended.
Yet I aspire to protect unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and even this aspiring mind cannot be grasped."
“World-Honored One!

This nature of the path to enlightenment is free from conceptual discrimination; it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. It is without seeing and without hearing, neither grasping nor abandoning, perfect, quiescent, and cannot be sought through characteristics, for it is free from conceptual proliferation.”

At that time, there were another three hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas in the assembly who rose from their seats, prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and having offered respectful praise, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We, too, shall protect the World-Honored One’s secret, profound, and difficult-to-understand Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which was attained over the course of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya nayuta koṭi kalpas; in future ages, we shall skillfully act for the sake of others, upholding, reciting, expounding its wondrous meaning, transcribing it, and reverently making offerings to it.”
When all the bodhisattvas had finished speaking these words, each removed the upper garment they were wearing and used it as an offering; having made this vow, they withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:

"You are able to fulfill vast compassion; if, in the future final age, there are sentient beings who do not delight in the True Dharma, you shall protect and uphold this Dharma at such a time, causing all sentient beings not to give rise to false views."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya prostrated himself before the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I vow that in this world of five turbidities and evil, I shall skillfully protect this samādhi so that it is not interrupted, and cause all sentient beings of wrong views and distracted minds to gradually awaken to and enter the most supreme and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna."
The World-Honored One again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:

"In this assembly now, three hundred and eighty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas abide in this Dharma; they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, giving rise to a heart of aspiration and joy, practicing and studying with diligence, vowing never to regress or abandon it."
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas whose minds are not yet firm, such that they are unable to receive and uphold this Dharma, nor do they take delight in it;

in the future final age of the five turbidities, they will be unable to protect and maintain the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cultivated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas and yuta-koṭi kalpas;
within this Dharma, they will instead give rise to disputes and various afflictions, being unable to sustain, delight in, or practice and study it.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
why is it that a bodhisattva does not take delight in the most supreme and excellent Dharma?"
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to cultivate such a practice of the Dharma, how many kinds of minds must they generate to achieve success?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!

Sons of good family, because bodhisattvas are hindered by innate notions of self and phenomena, as well as by ignorance and dullness, their wisdom, though present, is not clear. Consequently, they lack a resolute mind toward bodhi; they repeatedly retreat and abandon it, and for the most part do not find joy in it.
If there are bodhisattvas who wish to firmly seek and aspire to enter this supreme vehicle of the seal of wisdom of samādhi, they should give rise to seven kinds of resolve toward enlightenment.
What are the seven kinds?

First, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, did in the past when on the causal ground: he sought out spiritual friends, not sparing even his own body or life, seeking the path of the Buddha and resolving to attain bodhicitta.

Second, they give rise to the bodhicitta for the sake of lovingly delighting in the cultivation and study of all subtle and supreme dharmas, and for the sake of guarding them with single-minded devotion.

Third, seeing that all sentient beings undergo various sufferings and are distressed day and night without a time of liberation, one gives rise to great compassion with the universal desire to rescue and deliver them; for such reasons as these, one generates the bodhicitta.

Fourth, universally desiring to benefit all sentient beings without distinguishing between enemies and kin, so that they may all attain happiness and liberation through mastery—this is for the sake of such as these that one resolves upon bodhicitta.

Fifth, they universally practice joyful giving toward all sentient beings, employing skillful means to gather them in and cause them to be free from fear; they do not give rise to cowardice regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and for such purposes as these, they resolve upon bodhicitta.

Sixth, seeing all bodhisattvas resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), they feel joy and delight; they draw near to them and train under their guidance, resolving upon the mind of enlightenment together with those bodhisattvas.
Seventh, in order to hear of the Tathāgata’s preeminent physical marks and qualities, which are perfectly pure and supreme;
and in order to seek the stainless, supramundane fruits of holiness, one generates the bodhicitta.

"Good son! When a bodhisattva gives rise to these seven kinds of most excellent and sublime minds, they are able to gradually achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never abandoning sentient beings and always protecting the true Dharma."
These are called the seven ways of generating the bodhicitta.
Son of good family!
If bodhisattvas are skillfully able to cultivate the four immeasurable minds, study the profound Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and further accomplish five kinds of superior dharmas.
"These bodhisattvas who are thus endowed are called 'avaivartika' (non-retrogressive).
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the five dharmas by which one attains non-retrogression?
'Good son, first, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; one does not harbor intimacy toward one's own kin, nor does one feel aversion or abandon other sentient beings.'"
Second, upon seeing sentient beings obtain gain and offerings, he feels deep joy and praises them with kind words, without giving rise to feelings of resentment, envy, or affliction.

Third, regarding the subtle and supreme Dharma of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, they aspire to hear it and desire to proclaim it; wishing to protect and uphold such a treasury of the Dharma, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives as they widely disseminate it so that it continues without interruption.

Fourth, regarding all kinds of material wealth and necessities for life, they are free from stinginess and are able to bestow them upon all sentient beings; furthermore, they impartially and universally provide excellent food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, ensuring that all are fully satisfied.
Fifth, they joyfully delight in the supreme, victorious qualities of the Tathāgatas—the vast wisdom and secret dhāraṇīs—and diligently cultivate and study them.
"These are the five kinds of supreme dharmas of a bodhisattva; one should resolutely seek them with a mind that does not regress.
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
"Furthermore, there are five dharmas whose nature is rigid and stubborn, which can obstruct bodhi and prevent liberation."
What are the five dharmas?
First, being unable to understand the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Second, greedily seeking gain and offerings without satiety.
Third, they constantly harbor stinginess and cannot practice generous giving.
Fourth, they are deceitful and insincere, never ceasing such behavior.
Fifth, their mouths speak only of emptiness, yet they do not understand all phenomena.
Maitreya Bodhisattva!
These five dharmas, when habitually practiced, are stubborn and rigid; they obscure and obstruct bodhi, preventing the accomplishment of the unsurpassed holy fruit.

Furthermore, there are five other dharmas which, if bodhisattvas are able to fulfill them, will enable them to expound and explain the supreme Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, to cultivate it with firm resolve, and to enter the stage of the noble ones.
A bodhisattva such as this is called *avaivartika*.
What are the five dharmas?
First is non-self (*anātman*), which is to remain far removed from the bondage of signs and not to cling to self or other.
Second is the non-existence of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is far removed from attachment to the conventional and the essential nature maintained by the ultimate truth.
Third is the equality and non-duality of the nature of wisdom and its characteristics, free from all hatred and affection, tranquil and profoundly still.
Fourth, they do not cling to bodhi or sentient beings, nor are they deluded regarding good and evil, cause and effect, or the gradual stages [of practice].
Fifth, they thoroughly understand the distinct characteristics of the Tathāgata’s merits, rūpakāya, supernormal powers, transformations, attainment of enlightenment, and entry into parinirvāṇa.
“Good son! One who fully understands these five dharmas as they are is called an avaivartika (non-retrogressive) and is able to achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Sentient beings lacking wisdom falsely distinguish between what is Dharma and what is not;
they debate worldly conventions and investigate the beautiful and the ugly,
yet fail to guard their own actions of body, speech, and mind."
Those who cultivate with single-minded devotion, delighting in tranquility,
practicing ethical discipline and patience, and whose speech is always gentle,
are able to protect and uphold Bodhi.
Like a rhinoceros that delights in solitude, having abandoned the clamor of the crowd, one always finds joy in dwelling in empty stillness;
like a deer in the deep mountains, entirely free from all fears,
so too is the practitioner, unattached like the wind.
To uphold and protect the profound Dharma, they are able to relinquish even their own bodies and lives.
Their minds are free from desire; whether in motion or stillness, and in all their deeds, they act solely for the benefit of others. Their wisdom is ever-luminous and keen.
Those who are not deluded regarding the characteristics of objects, yet lack faith among sentient beings, cannot receive this Dharma;
they give rise to doubt at every contact and are incapable of awakening or understanding.
Acting perversely through false conduct, their minds are deranged and inverted.
Such deluded people are unable to guard this Dharma of Bodhi, nor do they delight in its cultivation.
I recall that in a past life, at the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I heard of this samādhi and resolved to practice it. Furthermore,
after the passing of more than hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas,
Furthermore, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, Whose name was Crest-Banner (Cūḍā-ketu).
For the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, He preached this samādhi.
At his first assembly for preaching the Dharma, There were eight billion [disciples].
Ten billion bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression;
in the second assembly, the number was seventy billion;
when he preached the Dharma in the third assembly, there were another seventy-three [billion].
Ten million bodhisattvas all dwell on the stage of non-retrogression.
That Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching; the radiance emitted from his body extends sixty yojanas in width.
Nine hundred thousand koṭis, having distanced themselves from all bonds of suffering,
all attained arhatship.
Known by the name Puṇyottama, they ruled over Jambudvīpa.
Calculating its extent by land measure, it was seven hundred thousand yojanas.
The king ruled over the four continents; his consorts and court ladies numbered sixty koṭis, and he had a thousand princes.
All marks are fully perfected;
the people are all happy. There are eight hundred koṭis of cities and gardens, filled with the most exquisite flowers and fruits.
All things were exquisitely adorned, decorated with mani-jewels like the realms of the devas;
yet within a dream, he heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world.
His name was Cūḍaketu.
Leading his retinue of ministers, officials, and people—
sixteen hundred koṭis— he came to where the Buddha was.
Having heard this samādhi,
the profound and true Dharma, his heart gave rise to great joy;
he immediately offered all the lands as alms to the Buddha.
And they regarded this as making offerings;
using the finest and most exquisite sandalwood, each constructed various vihāras,
complete with gardens and groves, and adorned with gold, silver, and all manner of rare treasures.
Adorned in various ways,
for eighty thousand years they dwelt securely within the Buddha-dharma;
able to remain far removed from all evils, toward both sentient and insentient beings, they were impartial.
Constantly cultivating supreme goodness, he renounces all worldly pleasures;
with a deep mind free from desire, he benefits his retinue solely through truthful speech.
The various offerings presented are beyond measure;
by making such offerings to the Buddha in pursuit of samādhi,
one is said to be born into the family of the Buddhas.
This most profound and subtle Dharma cannot be sought through abiding signs,
nor can it be attained by a deluded mind;
yet this samādhi is named the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom.
Having abandoned his kingdom to leave the household life,
he practiced samādhi for eighty thousand years, never once becoming weary or negligent throughout day and night.
Throughout a long period of time, the Buddha expounded the Dharma, bringing vast awakening to many.
Later, upon entering parinirvāṇa, the King constructed sixty-four koṭis of stūpas; each and every stūpa—
Each [offering] consisted of five hundred parasols, adorned with the seven precious jewels,
as well as various musical ensembles; they lit hundreds of thousands of fragrant lamps whose radiance shone everywhere, presenting all manner of ritual offerings.
All were extensively and magnificently prepared;
when their number was tallied, it was seventy-three thousand years.
He preached this samādhi, the peerless and sublime Dharma of signlessness.
Their minds dwell nowhere;
even when making offerings and offering praise, their hearts do not give rise to joy.
They remain far removed from all signs of existence as well as from all incantations and arts.
They constantly protect and uphold the True Dharma.
Seventy nayutas [of beings] abide securely in the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
tranquil and ever joyful, they remain steadfast in all points of training.
There is nothing that is not fully perfected;
the three karmas are entirely pure. Regarding all that has already been studied, they fix the mind upon it without interruption;
regarding the teachings not yet studied, [they apply themselves with diligence].
Exerting diligence in cultivation,
maintaining resolute conviction and mental retention, contemplating with constant mindfulness so as never to forget,
one remains far removed from all conceptual proliferation.
And with various divergent conceptions,
they practice the conduct of enlightenment in vain; though they teach and transform sentient beings,
they greedily seek fame and reputation, preaching the Dharma for the sake of gain and sustenance.
Abiding in the signs of all existence, they claim that everything is empty;
yet they do not truly understand the nature of emptiness—this is precisely what is called "attachment.
Their realization of the mind differs from their teaching; their livelihood is wrong and impure.
If one practices what is contrary to the Dharma, speaking only of emptiness with the mouth while the mind remains bound by signs—
if one cultivates such conduct, in the end nothing will be attained.
The Wheel-Turning King Puṇyottara was none other than the present Buddha Amitāyus of the Land of Peace and Bliss;
the thousand sons of that king were the thousand World-Honored Buddhas of this present Bhadrakalpa.
Those who previously heard the Dharma from me, Who at that time left the household life together with the King and became bhikṣus,
Numbering in the hundreds of billions (*koṭi-nayuta*), Within all the Buddha-dharmas—
Having left the household life, they hear the true Dharma; hearing it, they are able to understand it all.
Consequently, for immeasurable eons, they practice various skillful means and make offerings to all dharmas, yet they do not cling to the marks of bodhi.
Abiding securely within the limit of reality,
their merit and wisdom are equal; just as you have granted me this prediction that I shall attain Buddhahood in a future age under the name Śākyamuni.
