At that time, in the assembly was King Bimbisāra; the king’s queen was named Bhadrāśrī, also known as Gopikāprabhā—King Ajātaśatru was born of her. She rose from her seat, prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground, and paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Having thus paid homage, he knelt with both knees upon the ground, prostrated with palms joined, and with a serene countenance, praised the Buddha’s virtues with a sublime voice.
Furthermore, he offered hundreds of thousands of priceless jewels and exquisite garments to the World-Honored One as an act of worship.
Furthermore, he scattered five hundred flowers made of the seven precious gems into the air, where they formed a cloud-like canopy of flowers that completely covered the entire assembly.
Having performed these various offerings, Bhadrasri then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I contemplate that in the future age of turbidity and evil, sentient beings will have weak and inferior faculties of faith and their afflictions will increase.
I vow that they shall believe in, understand, receive, and uphold this most excellent Dharma-gate of samādhi.

If one sees someone who copies, upholds, hears, recites, explains, reveals, and guides others, causing it to be transmitted from person to person without interruption, so that all may see and hear it, give rise to faith and understanding, and practice with diligence.

Such a person is called a vessel of the Dharma; toward those who uphold it, I shall rejoice and praise them, attend upon and serve them, and provide them with all necessary requisites—food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—ensuring that no offerings fall short.

Furthermore, by means of the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they are further led to realization, so that their Mahāyāna lineage may swiftly reach maturity in the dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They do not falsely discriminate between emptiness and non-emptiness, for they understand that all phenomena are free from verbal attachment;
accordingly, they realize and practice without giving rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

For the sake of protecting the True Dharma, one should not begrudge even one's own body or life, let alone worldly material goods—the instruments that increase afflictions and perpetuate birth and death!
"You should only practice and study such a sublime dharma of samādhi!
Having spoken these words, he withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, eight thousand ladies of the inner palace of King Bimbisāra, having heard this teaching, each gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment). All of them took delight in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna and desired to learn how to dwell securely within such a sublime gateway of samādhi. Each rose from her seat, joined her palms in reverence, prostrated with her head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We shall all, in the future, during the final age of the Dharma’s decline, receive, uphold, and protect such a profound, perfect, and subtle Dharma; furthermore, we vow to provide offerings to and support those who receive and uphold it!”

At that time, six hundred thousand laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) from the kingdom of Magadha, having witnessed this event, were all filled with joy. They each likewise gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and with deep hearts they rejoiced in this Dharma of the *jñāna-mudrā-samādhi*, making this vow:
"We too wish that in the future, during the turbid and evil age, we may fully protect and uphold this sublime Dharma!"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the aspirations of heart and mouth held by the laymen and laywomen of Magadha, as well as the noble lady Kāñcanaprabhā Bhadrāśrī and her eight thousand palace attendants—who had with faith, understanding, and resolve received and upheld this sublime Dharma, practicing it for a long time without interval or interruption, and knowing that the fruit of all Buddhas arises from this Dharma—manifested joy and smiled with delight.

Because of this smile, hundreds of thousands of kinds of subtle and wondrous colored lights issued from the Buddha’s mouth—namely blue, yellow, red, white, and crystal—and these various colors and forms pervaded the entire world.
The sentient beings therein, beholding this radiance, were freed from all fear and tamed and subdued all the demonic adversaries of affliction.

This light shone upward as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), penetrating everywhere where the light of the sun and moon does not reach; it reached downward to all the great hells and evil destinies, causing their suffering and distress to cease, their impurities to be entirely removed, and all to attain purity.
The light circled back to the place where the Buddha was, circumambulated him to the right a thousand times, covered the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, and then vanished from sight.

At that time, the Lady Bhadraśrīkoṭikanakaprabhā, having seen this light and not yet understanding the purpose of the Tathāgata’s emission of light, rose from her seat, adjusted her robes and appearance, joined her palms in reverence, knelt on both knees, prostrated herself before the World-Honored One, and with diligent application of the three karmas, praised the Buddha’s virtues, speaking in verse:
“The distinctions of the Buddha’s virtues are boundless; Supreme within the three realms, there is none equal to you.

Like a flower in full bloom, radiating fragrance, Or like the moon’s reflection in the sky, already perfected— The Buddha-mind is equanimous, free from sorrow and joy; Why, then, do you manifest a smile now?
I now look up and conjecture the cause of your smile; you should proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
You, the Honored One of Ten Powers, who is fully endowed with peace and bliss, stand among the assembly like the moon among the stars.
The words and meanings you speak are rich and profound, serving as the eyes for all sentient beings throughout the worlds.
The Dharma is like a single rain, without distinction, yet it causes understanding to arise according to the various faculties and natures;
with a pure and resonant Brahma-voice and boundless merit, all who hear it are filled with joy.
By virtue of these supreme conditions for hearing the Dharma, we have attained unprecedented joys;
may the Buddha roar the lion’s roar, to eliminate all manner of karmic retributions.
Sentient beings who hear the Dharma all rejoice; they delight in the equal flavor of its various meanings.
Whether seeing, hearing, or upholding it themselves or others, they are able to understand it according to their faculties and the appropriate time.
From this, the bodhicitta is awakened, and one develops reverence for all that is heard;
with the eightfold perfect, untainted voice, it universally accords with the diverse inclinations and desires of infinite beings.
Among all the merits of expounding the Dharma, They accord with every number without contradiction;
Causing all sentient beings who receive the teaching To awaken to and enter it, their minds firm in hearing and retaining.
Afflictions shall not disturb their minds, causing them never to regress from what they have attained;
upholding the prohibitions and all codes of discipline, they are able to endure all adverse conditions even when encountered.
Far removed from worldly toil and free from all suffering, with body and mind dwelling in the bliss of quiescent extinction,
one should constantly apply oneself with diligence to contemplating and practicing these supreme deeds of enlightenment.
The Buddha’s body is like a mountain of exquisite gold, Also like a jeweled stupa, a mass of radiant light;
Like a lotus emerging from the water in full bloom— All who see or hear it gaze upon it with reverence.
Like the lion king when he sports, He roars a great sound that subdues all beasts;
I pray you will expound the causes and conditions of this smile, So that my assembly may have their doubts dispelled.
The Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena, In perfect accord with the signless, true reality;
He causes all sentient beings of diverse natures To each purify their three karmas until they are stainless.
Never abandoning sentient beings, he constantly protects and sustains them, Causing them to turn toward virtuous causes and obtain supreme fruits;
May all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, Upon hearing this, contemplate it and practice it correctly.
It subdues the heat of all afflictions; like drinking nectar, the mind becomes cool and clear.
Among all the sounds in the world, none can compare to the voice with which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.
Lutes, pipes, flutes, and horns; lutes with hollow gourds, drums, harps, and exquisite singing;
the striking of *gaṇḍī* staffs and the sounding of gongs and cymbals—all such instruments resound together.
The *jīvajīvaka*, *parapuṣṭa*, and *śuka* birds—all such flocks of birds sing in harmony.
The Buddha utters a subtle, wondrous, and soft voice, Whose manifold qualities no other sound can equal.
This assembly from the ten directions has gathered here, Differing in their adherence to what is right or wrong, and in their hearts' inclinations.
I pray that you will teach by skillful means according to what is appropriate, To subdue those among them who are stubborn and unruly.
May all cause their unwholesome minds to be reformed, And universally fulfill boundless, supreme, and wholesome vows.
Having come from koṭis of buddha-fields To hear the World-Honored One preach the Dharma,
May they now comprehend the sound of the True Dharma, And, free from all fears, attain peace and happiness.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will rain down the Dharma-rain, Compassionately expounding the unsurpassed Dharma;
May he fulfill the stainless voice, So that we may ultimately attain the fruit of Bodhi.
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the noble lady Bhadraśrīkoṭikanakaprabhā, the World-Honored One further spoke these verses to the assembled multitude:
"In immeasurable ages, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
there was once a Great Dharma King named Asaṃjñāpuṇyaprabha."
The Buddha’s lifespan is exceedingly long, seventy-six koṭis;
he transforms all four continents.
In that land, the assembly of śrāvakas is immeasurable in number.
By means of the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Wisdom, he guides the various classes of sentient beings.
His name was Victorious Wisdom (*Jñānavijaya*). The king had two consorts:
the first was named Imperial Banner (*Dhvaja*), and the second was known as Sunlight (*Sūryaprabhā*).
Having heard this gateway of the seal of wisdom, one should always exert oneself with diligence day and night,
assiduously cultivating all wholesome deeds for one *koṭī* of years;
and protect the eye of the True Dharma for sixty *koṭīs* of years.
Acting as a teacher and guide for the multitudes, he has, at the abodes of thirty billion immeasurable Buddhas,
accumulated all manner of merit; throughout immeasurable worlds,
his eye of Dharma constantly provides protection and salvation.
Thirty Ganges-sands of future Buddhas, throughout each and every world,
shall equally and universally protect and uphold this eye of the True Dharma, ensuring that it never be severed.
At that time, that King Jñānavara was none other than the present Buddha Akṣobhya.
Those pure assemblies in his gathering—the queen and her retinue—were each born together with him; such is the Buddha-field.
Guarding the Dharma with a tireless mind, one shall again, in successive times,
transform that female body into a male form and be born immediately in the immeasurable, blissful Buddha-world.
In this present age of the final dharma, you alone are virtuous and auspicious;
you are able to protect the Tathāgata’s Dharma, upholding it so that it is not destroyed.
You should employ the bodhicitta to pervade all Buddha-fields.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, may all beings be protected and saved.
May those who awaken to the Dharma be born together in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
sit upon thousand-petaled lotuses, and attain the physical marks and signs of all Buddhas.
Fully endowed with all adornments,
he shall again make offerings to the Buddhas; finally, in due succession,
during that Adornment Eon, he shall attain the unsurpassed path.
With this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they transmit it to all humans and devas,
causing them to resolve upon the Unsurpassed Mind and together protect the True Dharma.
In that land, one is free from the enmity of Māra and the karma of the three poisons.
No sinful transgressions arise, and all evils are entirely absent.
Not dwelling within a womb, they are born through pure transformation;
together with countless bodhisattvas, they have all gathered for this assembly.
There are no śrāvakas, nor even the mention of their names;
having distanced themselves from all adverse conditions, they constantly cultivate the practices of bodhi.
Having renounced fame and gain, they harbor no attachment to intimacy.
Sacrificing body, life, and wealth, he benefits all classes of sentient beings.
Through skillful means he preaches the Dharma, causing all universally to give rise to faith and understanding.
If there are those who can practice it, they shall attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed enlightenment.
Abiding within this Dharma, they do not seek worldly pleasures;
practicing exactly as taught, they pervade all Buddha-fields,
constantly generating a mind of reverence and upholding the teachings of all Buddhas.
For those who harbor jealousy, one should secretly protect and uphold [the teaching],
and with a heart of great compassion, instruct all sentient beings,
causing them to train in this way so that they may all be freed from every suffering and calamity.
Just as in times past, for the sake of seeking bodhi,
throughout koṭis of kalpas, I gave away my head, eyes, marrow, and brain,
as well as precious jewels, wives, and children, without any attachment to anything at all.
If within my Dharma one cannot give rise to true faith,
though they shave their hair and dye their robes, being foolish and forgetting the true nature of reality,
they greedily seek fame and wealth, preaching the Dharma for the sake of gain and sustenance.
Associating with those who lack discipline, Neglecting the upholding and recitation [of the teachings],
Though wishing to train as a śramaṇa, One fails in the conduct of a śramaṇa.
When the Buddha spoke these words, The assembly of humans and devas present—
There were eighty koṭis [of beings], all of whom gave rise to a heart of compassion;
thinking of such a person who was about to sink into the evil realms,
they spoke these words in unison:
“I vow that in the future, through the power of bodhicitta, I shall universally protect and uphold all with equanimity.
Having spoken these words, the trichiliocosm shook violently,
and the devas rained down a multitude of flowers.
Within this land, thorns and filth— by virtue of these supreme causes and conditions— all shall be utterly extinguished;
it will be no different from the heavens, pure and pristine throughout.
In future ages, there will be those who hear such a Mahāyāna as this; they shall attain the most supreme life of wisdom.
The multitudes of devas and humans in the ten directions will rejoice and pay them all respectful homage.
Praising the Mahāyāna sūtras and their various wondrous meanings,
all the dragon kings, yakṣas, and rākṣasas abandoned their poisonous and evil minds, and all paid them respectful homage.
If sentient beings in the final age, having heard this most supreme and profound Sūtra of the Seal of Wisdom, are able to believe and understand it,
the merit obtained by such persons shall now be briefly illustrated through analogy.
Suppose the number of Buddha-fields were like the sands of the Ganges,
and one were to fill them all with precious jewels to offer as a gift to the Buddhas;
by practicing such supreme deeds for kalpas exceeding the sands of the Ganges—
The merit one gains from that is not equal to hearing this gate of the seal of unsurpassed wisdom, opening it for others and expounding it;
the merit obtained thereby exceeds the former by immeasurable and boundless degrees.
This merit is formless and cannot be known by a conditioned mind. If,
through hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma of the subtle and wondrous seal of wisdom,
one gives rise to the bodhicitta and accords with all phenomena, [this merit is inconceivable].
Relying on what the Buddha has proclaimed, practice exactly as taught;
furthermore, in the final age, diligently observe and protect [the Dharma],
delighting in empty and quiet places, seeking liberation with a single mind.
Having accumulated immeasurable and supreme virtuous merits,
you constantly instruct all sentient beings through the three types of ethical discipline.
With a heart of love and compassion, you cherish them as a mother thinks of her child.
With a joyful and gentle voice, he teaches them to leave behind enmity and thieves.
Within the Buddha’s True Dharma, they do not give rise to inverted views;
benefiting both themselves and others, he swiftly leads them to Perfect Enlightenment.
If, regarding the seal-gate of vast wisdom within samādhi,
one is able to write it down, receive and uphold it, recite and correctly expound it,
and transmit it from one to another to sentient beings, so that both self and others attain understanding;
They shall likewise obtain all supreme and virtuous karmic fruits;
neither speech nor thought can reach them,
for such persons shall all be born in the peaceful and blissful lands of the Buddhas.
When the World-Honored One saw him, he conceived thoughts of kinship and friendliness;
with a heart of compassion, he protected him, and with joy, he accepted him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How many types of persons possessing the nature of the various vehicles are able to receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of the Samādhi-Wisdom Seal, so as to protect and maintain the True Dharma in future ages, to give rise to love and joy for that True Dharma, and to be able to produce faith, understanding, and a fondness for practicing this Tathāgata’s secret and profound Dharma-gate of the Wisdom Seal?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

"In that evil world of the five turbidities, the sentient beings are oppressed by incalculable sufferings. Only those bodhisattvas who, in this evil world, shoulder the true Dharma and give rise to faith and understanding are truly rare."

Furthermore, those sentient beings in the final age constantly hear of strife, false speech, and frivolous talk; some may even destroy their roots of goodness, such that they are unable to comprehend or understand any of the teachings within this most supreme Dharma-gate of the Seal of Wisdom.

Only the Bodhisattvas, amidst this world of five corruptions when the Dharma is about to perish, regard suffering sentient beings with loving-kindness and compassion, benefiting and gathering them in through various skillful means.

Thus, these people, being oppressed by suffering and affliction, if they were not received, transformed, and guided by Bodhisattvas, would be unable to believe in, understand, receive, uphold, read, or recite the profound Dharma.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”

Out of compassion and for the sake of the peace and happiness of sentient beings, he proclaims such sublime Dharma, the nectar of immortality, so that all sentient beings of the future may attain this benefit, give rise to a heart of empathetic sorrow, and joyfully cultivate it.

If that bodhisattva attains this Dharma-gate, they will accord with the supreme and most excellent conduct of the Tathāgata; being firm and resolute in their pursuit, they shall never destroy the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, quickly realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and entering into harmony with the Buddha-way through corresponding superior practices without ever falling back or abandoning them.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:

“If there are bodhisattvas who, throughout a hundred past lives, have personally approached, revered, served, and made offerings to Buddhas; who have resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) and planted various roots of goodness and the foundations of all virtues—yet, in that future age of turbidity and evil, they are unable to believe or understand this vast, unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous meaning of bodhi, and cannot enter into this Dharma-gate of the Seal of Vast Wisdom.”
Furthermore, Maitreya!

If there is a bodhisattva who, in the past, in the presence of a thousand World-Honored Ones, has resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, drawn near to them with reverence, planted various roots of goodness, and established the foundations of virtue—such a bodhisattva, even if they encounter a virtuous friend in that future age of five turbidities and resolve upon the mind of enlightenment, will nonetheless be unable to comprehend the subtle principles of the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Vast Wisdom. They will repeatedly give rise to doubts and hesitations, feel no joy or affection for it, and will be unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or disseminate it; nor can they explain it for others so as to inspire faith and understanding.
Furthermore, Maitreya!

There are also bodhisattvas who, throughout the past, have encountered hundreds of thousands of buddhas, having generated the mind of enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, and established the foundations of all virtues. Although they may encounter virtuous friends in that future age of turbidity and evil and generate the mind of enlightenment, their faith and understanding regarding this vast, profound, and supreme Dharma-door of the Seal of Wisdom will be weak and inferior. They will be unable to penetrate its deep and far-reaching meaning, nor will they be able to receive, uphold, read, recite, praise to others, or explain such unsurpassed, vast, and profound benefits of enlightenment.
Furthermore, Maitreya!

Suppose there is a bodhisattva who, from the past, has generated the mind of enlightenment and planted various roots of goodness and established the foundations of merit under as many as one koṭi of Buddhas. Although such a person may, in the future period of the final age, encounter virtuous friends and generate the mind of enlightenment, and although they may hear, write down, recite, delight in, and uphold this dharma-gate of the vast, subtle, and most supreme Seal of Wisdom, they will not yet be able to understand its profound meaning. They will be unable to analyze and explain it for others; they will not have definitively sealed their resolve in the supreme truth of the great mind of enlightenment, nor will they have attained realization in this samādhi-gate of the Seal of Wisdom.
Furthermore, Maitreya!

Suppose there is a bodhisattva who, in the presence of those thirty koṭis of World-Honored Ones in the past, has generated the mind of enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, and established the foundations of all virtues. Although such a person may encounter virtuous friends in the future final age, generate the mind of enlightenment, and hear this Dharma-gate of the Seal of Vast Wisdom, they will be able to hear, recite, receive and uphold, copy, circulate, and explain it for others; yet, because they lack a resolute mind to maintain and authenticate the method of the *jñānamudrā-samādhi*, they will be unable to accomplish the benefit of true reality.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

If there should be a bodhisattva who, in the presence of eighty koṭis of World-Honored Ones, hears this supreme dharma of samādhi and practices it as taught, and furthermore is able to transform and benefit all classes of sentient beings, causing them all to believe and accept it; and if, in the presence of those Buddhas, they resolve upon bodhicitta, plant various roots of goodness, and establish the foundations of merit; then, in that future age of the final dharma, by the power of their bodhicitta, they will be able to understand, receive and uphold, read and recite, copy, circulate, and explain to others this vast and profound Dharma-door of the Seal of Wisdom, taking deep delight in it with a sincere heart, being capable of protecting and upholding it so that it may be swiftly brought to fulfillment."
Having thus correctly understood this subtle gate of samādhi, one attains complete penetration into all phenomena.

Furthermore, within the vast Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi, one becomes free from all conceptual discrimination, subdues all evil Māras and adversaries, and destroys all unwholesome karmic obstructions. Regarding all causes of suffering created throughout immeasurable kalpas that were destined to yield retribution in future lives, one attains liberation from them all.

Furthermore, having created unwholesome causes in the past, when they reach this later evil age in which the Dharma is about to perish, their wholesome minds will be weak and inferior; they will destroy the True Dharma, take pleasure in and cling to the teachings of non-Buddhists and worldly conventions, increase frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), engage in unlawful conduct, utter meaningless speech, and fail to distinguish between the noble and the base. These many evil sentient beings will be full of greed and craving; seeing [the Dharma], they will show no respect, but instead treat it with contempt, insult, and humiliation, such that they will lack everything they require for themselves.
Thus, through the power of the great merit of realizing the supreme Dharma in this single lifetime, the causes of suffering are all extinguished.

Furthermore, by virtue of the roots of goodness accumulated from having approached and made offerings to all the Buddhas mentioned above in the past, one generates the bodhicitta within that future final age, is able to uphold this most excellent Dharma-gate of samādhi, becomes free from the bonds of suffering, attains non-retrogression, remains firm in the three karmas, gives rise to no distraction, and diligently strives toward the holy fruit of Bodhi.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

If there are bodhisattvas who, having committed unwholesome karma in the past, ought to fall into the evil realms, yet during that future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, hear this Dharma-gate and joyfully accept and uphold it—by these causes and conditions, whether they are tormented by the convergence of illness and fear, their karmic offenses from previous lives will immediately be extinguished."
They are deficient in their faculties and undergo various sufferings;
they are born into families of wrong views and dwell among the ignorant and foolish;
they are born into lowly families and are made to serve others.
Born into a poor family, one lacks sufficient food and clothing;
born into a stingy and greedy family, one is unable to provide relief;
and if one has anything to say, people do not believe or accept it.
Subjected to royal law, one encounters hostile enemies;
abandoned by kin and friends, the mind is filled with much sorrow and affliction;
and in the assembly of the Dharma of compassion, many obstacles and hindrances arise.
Even if he preaches the Dharma at will, people take no pleasure in hearing it;
as for the necessities of life—food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and attendants—he does not encounter those who provide them;
the poor seek his company, while the wealthy and powerful abandon him.
Or they may be harassed, disturbed, envied, or harmed by evil persons;
the wholesome dharmas they cultivate fail to increase;
or they may see various evil omens in their dreams.
Because they are oppressed by these minor sufferings, the karmic offenses of previous lives are immediately extinguished.
Once the karmic obstructions have been extinguished, even if they encounter adverse conditions or hostile enemies, those cannot cause them harm;
and although they remain in the company of Māras and do not distance themselves from them, they are able to clearly understand the realms of all Māras.
He has no attachment or delight in fame or gain;
he does not take pleasure in being approached by others, nor in being honored, respected, or praised;
he cultivates all wholesome practices and bestows gifts upon sentient beings, seeking liberation without giving rise to stinginess.
One guards the śīla without any violation;
one cultivates the practice of kṣānti to benefit sentient beings by uprooting their suffering and bestowing happiness;
one cultivates the practice of vīrya to exert the three karmas, diligently seeking all that is wholesome and remaining free from all evil desires.
Cultivating meditative concentration so that distraction does not arise;
awakening to the nature of all phenomena through great wisdom;
and benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings through skillful means and the power of vows.
Hearing immeasurable teachings, their minds never forget them;
they cultivate various kinds of goodness for the benefit of sentient beings;
and they harbor no longing for the fruits of worldly pleasure.
"May all sentient beings swiftly ascend to the other shore.

Furthermore, Maitreya, those bodhisattvas have, in the past, in the presence of hundreds of World-Honored Ones, resolved their minds on Bodhi with true equanimity; they have planted various roots of goodness, established the foundations of myriad virtues, and become free from the bonds of all suffering."

Because they come to harass and harm the evil sentient beings of the final age, these beings are unable to believe, understand, or practice this; how much less could the evil sentient beings of the final age—who have not planted roots of goodness and are deluded and distracted—be able to awaken!
Therefore, in the final age, those who are unwholesome will be unable to believe in, accept, or practice according to principle this most excellent and profound Dharma.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!"

If bodhisattvas can develop profound faith and understanding in these teachings, maintaining firm resolve, donning the armor of patience, subduing all Māras, practicing for a long duration, protecting and upholding them without yielding to despondency, then vast wisdom and immeasurable wholesome dharmas will arise from this teaching; they shall single-mindedly aspire to unsurpassed enlightenment, remaining in constant accord with it, steadfast and never forsaking it.

Furthermore, in the future, they shall expound the sublime meaning with tireless diligence, ultimately upholding this supreme dharma-gate of samādhi; they shall thoroughly comprehend all wholesome and unwholesome deeds, dwelling securely within the Dharma and zealously cultivating all practices.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four;
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Western Heaven Treasure-Wheel Great Master, the Imperially Invested Purple-Robed Śramaṇa.
Translated by Jin Zongchi and others by imperial decree.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and sixty inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, serving as the leaders among the great assembly, joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha in unison, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!

Having now heard such a subtle and supreme Dharma, we shall firmly protect and preserve it in the future; we shall teach all sentient beings to give rise to unsurpassed wisdom, and practice this supreme Dharma according to its teaching. We shall distance ourselves from all evils, refrain from arrogance and haughtiness, and be free from deceit, crookedness, and the mind of love or hatred. Toward the spheres of self and others, as well as enemies and kin, we shall maintain complete equanimity. Regarding the essential Dharma-seals of the dhāraṇī-wisdom obtained by the Tathāgatas over countless koṭis, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, we shall joyfully accept, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite them, even causing them to be transmitted and circulated from one to another in succession without interruption.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas King of Joy, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and the sixty inconceivable Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas— who had generated the supreme resolve to protect the True Dharma for the sake of the peace and happiness of sentient beings— the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly with a pure voice,
speaking in verse: “Planting all roots of goodness and free from flattery and pride,
Abiding in tranquility, devoid of all evils, With deep patience firm and unshakable, Always maintaining right mindfulness toward supreme wisdom.”
Abiding thus, endowed with great power, one is able to guard the accumulation of the wealth of Dharma;
free from all evil conduct and its afflictions, one does not act for the sake of fame or gain.
Free from contention and detached from defilement, universally equal like space—
such a person is able to guard [this samādhi] and will gradually attain this samādhi.
With profound patience and firm resolve, they delight in Bodhi; day and night they exert themselves without slackening or ceasing.
Guarding their majestic deportment and remaining free from all evils, they cause their understanding of the most profound Dharma to increase.
Regarding all the wealth and treasures of the world, And one's kinsmen and relatives, one feels no attachment;
Having completely renounced them and abandoned all clinging, With a mind of equanimity free from notions of enemy or kin,
Such a person attains accomplishment In the unsurpassed great jewel of samādhi.
Exerting diligent effort throughout day and night, one is able to give rise to awakening regarding this Dharma;
by honoring and revering spiritual friends and joyfully praising this samādhi,
one can understand the inexhaustible phenomena of the world, and thus remains unattached to defiled objects.
Sealing all phenomena with patience, the mind is pure, Like the light of a hundred koṭis of suns;
The radiance of wisdom destroys all darkness, Able to enter into the meaning of such profound dharmas.
This person’s wisdom and understanding are free from all attachments, Like the sun and moon dwelling in the void;
As firm and thick as the Great Snowy Mountains, They press down upon the great earth and can adorn it.
Also like Śakra, Brahmā, or a Wheel-Turning King, Possessing great majestic deportment, they are honored by all people.
He is also called the Unsurpassed Great King of Physicians, Able to eliminate all manner of suffering from disease.
Exhausting all karmic obstructions so that the mind becomes pure, He crushes and destroys the entire retinue of Māra.
Gradually accomplishing the knowledge of others' minds, He discerns and distinguishes all various types of mental states.
Recalling those nayutas of past eons, he has extinguished the blazing fires of affliction.

This person is praised by the Sugata; having realized the principle of the emptiness of bodhi, he is able to enter the gateway of the Tathāgata’s seal of wisdom and obtain all boundless treasuries of jewels.
Thoroughly realizing that names and signs lack intrinsic nature, One does not cling to emptiness or existence, abiding in the Middle Way;
Observing the five aggregates as like dust or illusions, One certifies that the four elements are not real in essence.
All conditioned phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing; The deluded mind creates them, forming the cycle of saṃsāra.
The nature of the samādhi of supreme wisdom is quiescent; Free from all conceptualization, it is inconceivable.
Serenely, it is as it has been from the beginning throughout the three times; Without going, without coming, and without movement.
If one sees people of wrong views in the final age, who cling to emptiness and existence within the Buddha’s True Dharma,
and yet have no realization of this [truth], claiming instead, "I have attained the emptiness of the nature of phenomena"—
these only increase the views of sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from the bodhicitta life after life.
Furthermore, I see some who follow and study [the path], weeping with tears and their hair standing on end in grief.
Moreover, in the final age, there will be many of the Śākya clan who possess all manner of decline and lack dignified deportment;
though they have left the home life seeking bodhi, they do not abide securely in that bodhi.
Violating the precepts and destroying right view, they ruin their dignified conduct; day and night they associate with those who are unwholesome.
Out of greed for gain, offerings, and the necessities of life, whatever they acquire they give back to their kinsmen.
Like one crossing the great ocean who loses their flotation bag, they will surely gaze from afar at the further shore.
Those who belong to the Supreme Vehicle, the true sons of the Śākya, renounce all such worldly things;
like a lotus emerging from the mud, their essential nature is pure and unstained.
I now instruct you, King Pramudita: you should constantly guard yourself with right mindfulness;
subdue delusive thoughts to give rise to true wisdom. Seeking this and endowed with all virtues, practice with diligence and without indolence; such a person is called a child of the Buddhas.
For example, like the seeds of worldly grains and wheat, In number as many as the sands of the Ganges and nayutas,
If these seeds were sown in fertile fields, Producing one another in succession for immeasurable eons,
The resulting grain and fruit would be beyond measure; Even calculation and analogy could not reach it.

Thus it continues in succession throughout the eastern direction; the same applies to as many varieties as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, even unto the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—the seeds sown therein are without distinction.
Suppose there were as many such beings as there are Buddhas, and each Buddha possessed a hundred heads,

with each head manifesting a hundred tongues; even if they were to praise the Tathāgata’s samādhi together throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they still could not exhaustively describe it.
Like taking mustard seeds to compare with Mount Sumeru, or like using a blade of slender grass to rival the realm of space;
or as if taking a single drop of water from the tip of a hair to set against the four boundless oceans— so too,
when these merits are weighed together, they are like numbers that calculation cannot reach.
"One should diligently practice and study this profound sutra for a long time.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and sixty inconceivable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, gave rise to the firm mind of great bodhicitta; with leaping joy and diligent effort, they addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!"

Regarding all the meanings of the profound Dharma—the ultimate truth and the most supreme nirvāṇa—although we in this assembly have conceived faith, we have not yet been able to understand them deeply.
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this for our sake!

At that time, the World-Honored One, with a single perfect voice, addressed the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and sixty inconceivable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, saying: “Good sons!

"Such supreme dharmas are originally quiescent, free from all conceptual discrimination, and cut off from all proliferations; they exist only as provisional names and expressions, revealed and proclaimed through conventional designations.
The Bodhisattvas said, "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!"
"How is it that this Dharma is free from all conceptualization and transcends all discursive proliferation, yet employs provisional verbal expressions to manifest it through skillful means?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"Although such a supreme Dharma is expressed through words, its essence cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is without conceptualization."
Why is the essence of this dharma unattainable?
Because this supreme dharma is without cultivation and without action, it is unattainable.
Why is this dharma without cultivation and without action?
Because this supreme dharma is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, it is not something produced through cultivation.
Why is this dharma without arising or ceasing?
Because the nature of this supreme dharma is free from the grasped object (*grāhya*) and is also not the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), it is therefore without arising or ceasing.
How is it that this dharma is without grasper and grasped?
Because this supreme dharma has no abiding and no location.
How is it that this dharma has no place of abiding?
Because this supreme dharma has the characteristic of being unchanging, it has no place of abiding.
Why does this dharma have the characteristic of being unchanging?
Because this supreme dharma is neither "that" nor "this," it is therefore unchanging.
How is it that this dharma is neither "that" nor "this"?
Because this supreme dharma is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
How is it that this dharma is neither conditioned nor unconditioned?
This is because this supreme dharma is neither false nor real.
Why is this dharma neither false nor real?
Because this supreme dharma is neither mind nor non-mind.
Why is this dharma neither mind nor non-mind?
Because this supreme dharma cannot be discerned.
Why is this dharma indiscernible?
Because this supreme dharma is devoid of any transformation of consciousness.
How is it that this dharma is devoid of any transformation of consciousness?
Because this supreme dharma is neither associated nor dissociated [with consciousness].
Why are these dharmas neither associated nor dissociated?
Because this supreme dharma is equal in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this dharma equal in its intrinsic nature?
Because this supreme Dharma cannot be sought through signs.
Why can this Dharma not be sought through signs?
Because this supreme Dharma lacks the characteristic of abiding.
Why is this dharma without the characteristic of abiding?
Because this supreme dharma lacks any intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Why does this dharma lack an intrinsic characteristic?
Because this supreme dharma is by nature empty and quiescent.
Why is this dharma by nature empty and quiescent?
Because this supreme dharma is free from defilement and attachment.
Why is this dharma free from attachment?
Because this supreme dharma is free from verbal expression and is pure. Good son!

Because this supreme Dharma is free from all conceptual discrimination, without cultivation, and without action, and because it is even beyond verbal expression and is pure by nature, it is called nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and sixty inconceivable numbers of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Such a supreme Dharma is difficult for people to understand, World-Honored One!
All dharmas enter the nature of the Dharma-realm; they are ultimately unattainable."
"How should we, such as ourselves, protect this Dharma-nature?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Rājavikrāmin, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and sixty inconceivable Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."
Such a supreme dharma is inconceivable, free from all conceptualization and proliferation.
If one gives rise to conceptual thoughts or proliferation regarding this dharma, then the dharma becomes dualistic.
If phenomena were dualistic, they would fall into arising and ceasing. Why is this?
This unsurpassed Dharma, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), is neither subject to arising nor subject to ceasing.
"To understand in this way is what is called 'guarding.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse for the sake of the bodhisattvas:
"The supreme dharma of non-action is not merely empty; It is free from all verbal expression and conceptual discrimination."
If there are those who, having attained the Dharma, cling to the two extremes, this is called the conceptual proliferation of various discursive elaborations;
such people do not accord with this Dharma, but only serve to increase their defiled wisdom.
This Dharma is signless and free from both aversion and attachment; it transcends all seeking and is without anything to be attained.
If one says of oneself, "I am patient with emptiness," one gives rise to conceptualization and various proliferations (*prapañca*).
Those very natures of emptiness cannot be apprehended, for they are difficult to fathom with a conceptualizing mind.
If one is free from doubt and slander regarding all phenomena, this is called "non-retrogression";
having severed the bonds of affliction and attained liberation, one possesses the patient acceptance of the mind-seal within this supreme Dharma.
If a person falsely understands and gives rise to discrimination, seeking and deliberating, they lose right understanding.
They weigh all phenomena and become attached to existence and emptiness; yet essence and appearance are fundamentally non-dual.
Using wisdom to seek wisdom is impossible to attain, for outside of wisdom there is no other wisdom.
He expounds the characteristics of saṃsāra and conditioned phenomena; such "wisdom" is not true wisdom, for it deludes one regarding the true void.
If one claims even a fraction of these things exists substantially, they become subject to arising and ceasing due to false conceptualization.
If one realizes the ultimate reality, one will know that all dharmas are fundamentally and eternally abiding.
Fools, through deluded conceptualization, undergo the cycle of transmigration; seeking nirvana out of weariness with birth and death, they increase their views of a self and its distinctions.
The wise understand that phenomena are non-dual: clarity and ignorance are fundamentally of the same essence. It is only because of lack of faith that they harbor fear and trepidation.
Such a person stubbornly clings to extreme views, increasing the proliferation of conceptual elaborations;
by declaring that conditioned phenomena are called nirvāṇa, they bring about the destruction of the true Dharma.
Mind and non-mind lack intrinsic nature, and that intrinsic nature is not mind either;
all phenomena are fundamentally without marks, beyond words and speech, serenely empty.
Phenomena arise from conditions and are not real; The cessation of all phenomena is likewise not the ultimate truth.
The eight truths and four truths clarify the conventional and the absolute; They are also called the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful means.
The Tathāgata’s true wisdom is ungraspable, and so too are all the dharmas he has taught.
Just as a physician treats various ailments by prescribing remedies according to each specific illness without attachment,
if one can give rise to awakening in this way, such a person is called a son of the Sugata.
The intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa is entirely equal, Vast as the great void, without limit or boundary.
The noble wisdom of the three vehicles is identical to nirvāṇa; It neither decreases nor increases, and is free from conceptual proliferation.
In the true dharma-realm, there is not a single sentient being, Nor is there a single word that can be spoken.
Sentient beings cling to their own discursive minds, Claiming them to be nirvana, though they abide nowhere;
Through ignorance and deluded thoughts, they bind themselves to saṃsāra, Where afflictions, karma, and birth-suffering perpetually continue.
The single truth of reality is free from views; alternatively, it is spoken of as fourfold according to circumstances.
Because there is the retribution of suffering, the cause is called "origination"; because of the principle of cessation, the truth of the path is elucidated.

Sentient beings in the final age harbor many delusive thoughts; they leave the home life not for the sake of pure conduct, but because of fame and profit they violate their dignified demeanor, and because they accumulate afflictions they give rise to strife and litigation.
The bhikṣus who cultivate merit can achieve this sublime Dharma;
remaining far removed from fame and the necessities of life, they delight in dwelling in araṇyas, free from seeking.

Just as a rhinoceros horn dwells alone upon the mountain, Contemplating such a samādhi, The eighty koṭis of the Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings Bestow their grace through a heart of loving-kindness upon the practitioner.
When the devas behold this, they all rejoice; They conceal their forms and constantly provide protection day and night.
Wisdom shatters darkness like the light of the sun; it gives birth to the supreme Dharma, which is like nectar.
Those who receive it possess the gateway of the seal of wisdom, and in their dreams they constantly meet with all Buddhas.
"You all should harbor courageous minds and practice with firm resolve, without ever retreating or abandoning your efforts.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying: "Mañjuśrī!"

If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment, they should practice and study in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom;
if they wish to accomplish the eighty minor marks of a Tathāgata, they should practice and study in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom;
if they wish to accomplish the eighteen unique and supreme qualities of a Tathāgata, they should practice and study in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom.

Desiring to accomplish the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four immeasurable minds—great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity—one should practice and train in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom;
desiring to accomplish the five eyes of all Buddhas, one should practice and train in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom;

desiring to obtain the vast lifespan, various adornments, sublime buddha-fields, and sovereign majestic power of all Buddhas, one should practice and train in accordance with this profound Dharma of the Seal of Samādhi Wisdom.

Desiring to bring all great Bodhisattvas and those Śrāvakas of sharp faculties to fulfillment; desiring to attain the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body, the vast dhāraṇīs, and the supreme and wondrous Dharma-gates; and desiring to understand the distinctions among the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, their mental activities, and their faculties and natures—endowed with supernormal powers, unimpeded eloquence, and a thorough comprehension of all phenomena—one should practice and train in accordance with this samādhi.
Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains correspondence with these samādhis, they will fully possess all such various merits and accomplish the unsurpassed Great Dharma of Bodhi.
That which is the basis of all phenomena is called the Unsurpassed Way;
wisdom that transcends the world is titled Perfectly Complete Enlightenment;
and that whose intrinsic nature is quiescent is named the Tathāgata.

As it is said, practicing without peer—because it is not equal to anything else—it is without arising and without cessation; it is the ultimate transcendence of the world, free from all verbal expression, and is called the First Truth.
The truth of ultimate reality is indestructible, steadfast, and disciplined; this is called the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and supreme dharma. Mañjuśrī!

By virtue of having cultivated and dwelled in this profound Dharma of the Wisdom-Seal Samādhi in the past, I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and received the prediction of my future enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and received the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*), how did he practice various difficult deeds and ascetic austerities throughout immeasurable kalpas within saṃsāra to achieve the attainment of bodhi?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"In the past, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, I matured the pure roots of goodness of all sentient beings. Through the power of great vows, over immeasurable time, I diligently practiced asceticism to transform and benefit sentient beings. According to their faculties—whether superior, middling, or inferior—I caused each to awaken to and enter the teachings and principles of the Three Vehicles, so that through gradual cultivation they attained realization."
“Mañjuśrī! At that time, by means of these vows and practices, I attained both awakening and nirvāṇa.
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one desires to be in accord with this Dharma and attains the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata,
the hundreds of millions of World-Honored Ones of the ten directions will all come to protect those who practice it."
If one can understand all the wondrous meanings within the profound Dharma of the Deathless, this is called the dhāraṇī of total retention; those who practice it shall all attain it.
Understanding words and sounds extinguishes all sins; it can shatter attachments and untie all bonds.
Nirvāṇa is without birth and without cessation; it has no going, no coming, and no place of abiding.
Adorned with the ten powers and all the marks and signs of excellence, Accomplishing all the merits of a Buddha,
With the perfect and pure voice of liberation, Universally responding to immeasurable sentient beings—
The sounds he utters can be fully understood, And all who hear them are filled with joy.
Far removed from wrong views and free from conceptualization, supremely pure and utterly stainless—
one who can train in accordance with this sutra will ultimately attain the path to enlightenment.
If a person, during those twenty-one days, contemplates this Dharma with a single-minded focus,
does not give rise to indolence or abandon their kin, practices day and night until it increases,
cultivates loving-kindness and compassion while remaining far removed from envy, and guards the precepts so as to sever all disputes—
Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, with a profound heart of joy they are ever liberated, far removed from the conditioned arising of all formations.
Like a lotus flower, they are unstained by attachment; firm and steadfast, they do not give rise to craving, just as a bird remains free from its bonds.
When this most supreme Dharma-gate was attained, the trichiliocosm shook in every direction;
the devas vied with one another to play exquisite music, scattering powdered incense and aloeswood,
hundreds of thousands of banners, streamers, and celestial robes, as well as pure flower garlands and necklaces.
Crown of mani-jewels and precious parasol, Adorned everywhere with interlaced golden bells;
All the devas perform songs and dances.
The community of bhikṣus and upāsakas, Along with bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās—
Each one removed their own exquisite upper robe And scattered it over the Buddha as an offering;
With reverent praise and focused contemplation, They vowed to seek this unsurpassed path.
I have preached such a profound Dharma, which gives rise to the bodhicitta that never regresses.
Those in this assembly, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who believe and understand it, shall all ultimately attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Furthermore, the future multitudes in all other lands, hearing of this Dharma in succession, will rejoice in their hearts.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of sentient beings each leaped for joy and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, eighty nayuta numbers of great bodhisattvas, having heard this Dharma, attained non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, sixty-three koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Additionally, sixty-three koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained samādhi.
Innumerable sentient beings attained the fruits of sainthood.
The great bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions realized such a Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (*jñānamudrā*).

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, sixty inconceivable numbers of bodhisattvas—headed by the Bodhisattva King of Joy, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī—as well as the great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, together with Lady Bhadraśrī-kanakaprabhā, the great śrāvakas, all the devas and humans of the fourfold assembly in the world, the gandharva kings, the asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
